proposals.new_text:
---
title: "Why do I spend more every time I earn more, and still feel behind?"
pubDate: "2026-07-13"
description: "Earning more did not create the breathing room you expected. Here is what is actually happening and what it costs you over time."
tags: ["money behaviour", "money worship", "spending patterns"]
---

You got the pay rise. You took on the extra client. The number went up.

And somehow, at the end of the month, the account looks roughly the same as before.

This is not a discipline problem. It is a pattern that has its own internal logic, and once you can see the logic, you can do something about it.

When income rises and spending rises to meet it almost immediately, it usually means that money is doing a particular job in your life: it is standing in for security, status, or proof that the effort is worth it. Spending the uplift feels like collecting on a debt that was owed to you. You worked hard. You earned the reward.

The problem is that the account balance never becomes the thing that settles the feeling. So the target keeps moving. Another raise. Another good month. Then it will feel like enough.

I had a version of this myself. I was earning well by the standards of where I grew up, and I had almost nothing saved. Not because I was struggling. Because every time money arrived, I found a use for it that felt entirely reasonable in the moment. A better flat. A trip I had been putting off. Gear for the gym. Each one justified. All of them, collectively, adding up to a position I was quietly embarrassed about.

The shift was not about spending less. It was about noticing what I was asking money to confirm about me.

If you recognise this pattern, the useful question is not "where can I cut?" It is: what is the spending actually for? Not the category. The function.

That question is worth sitting with before you build any kind of plan. A plan built on top of an unexamined pattern just gets spent around.

---
Joel Burgess, MSc Behavioural Economics | Qualified Financial Planner
